items.readable_text:
Content:
Given a dataset of paired numerical observations [MATH: (x,y)] and the corresponding linear regression model [MATH: \widehat{y} =f(x),] the residual for a particular observation [MATH: (x, y)] is defined as

Content:
[MATH: Residual|= Actual − Estimated; = y − f(x); = y − y^(^).]
We subtract the estimated value predicted by the model from the actual observed value.

Content:
To illustrate this concept graphically, consider the following example.

Content:
The owner of an ice cream shop keeps track of the average daily temperature [MATH: x] (measured in [MATH: ^\circ \mathrm{F}]) and the resulting daily ice cream sales [MATH: y] (in dollars). The scatter plot for several randomly selected days and the corresponding linear regression line are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/30abe98c5af06d6c97f71fdff2d46de1]

Content:
Suppose the equation of the regression line is
[MATH: y= 2.5 x +165.]

Content:
Let's use our regression line to compute the residual of the point with coordinates [MATH: \color{red}(82, 360)] (shown in red on our graph).

Content:
First, notice that since the highlighted data point has coordinates [MATH: {\color{red}(82, 360)},] our actual value is [MATH: y = {\color{red}360}.]

Content:
Next, we compute the predicted value using our linear regression model:

Content:
[MATH: y^(^)|= 2.5x + 165; = 2.5(82) + 165; = 370]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/933fa790d41a0d3a9e82f9542ab264cc]

Content:
Finally, we compute the residual:

Content:
[MATH: Residual|= Actual − Estimated; = y − y^(^); = 360 − 370; = − 10.]

Content:
The residual tells us that the linear model overestimates the true volume of ice cream sales by [MATH: \[math]10] when the outside temperature is [MATH: 82^\circ\,\textrm{F}.]

sections.normalized_html: Consider the data sets [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] of paired observations. The equation of the corresponding linear regression line for this data is [MATH: y=0.5x+7.] According to the model, what is the residual at [MATH: x=6] if the actual value of [MATH: y] corresponding to this value of [MATH: x] is [MATH: 12?]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the data sets [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] of paired observations. The equation of the corresponding linear regression line for this data is
[MATH: y=0.5x+7.]
According to the model, what is the residual at [MATH: x=6] if the actual value of [MATH: y] corresponding to this value of [MATH: x] is [MATH: 12?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The residual equals the difference between the actual value of the dependent variable and the value estimated using the linear regression model:

[MATH: \textrm{Residual} = \text{Actual} - \textrm{Estimated}]

First, we compute the predicted value using our linear regression model:

[MATH: y^(^)|= 0.5x + 7; = 0.5(6) + 7; = 10]

Therefore, the residual is

[MATH: Residual|= Actual − Estimated; = y − y^(^); = 12 − 10; = 2.]

sections.readable_text: We should be aware of the following interpretations for residual plots:

sections.normalized_html:
• Any point above the horizontal axis represents a positive residual. A positive residual means that the regression model underestimates the observed value for [MATH: y] at this point.

  • Any point below the horizontal axis represents a negative residual. A negative residual means that the regression model overestimates the observed value for [MATH: y] at this point.

- Any point below the horizontal axis represents a negative residual. A negative residual means that the regression model overestimates the observed value for [MATH: y] at this point.

sections.normalized_html: Residual plots can also be used to assess whether a trend line is a "good" fit for the corresponding data:
sections.readable_text: Residual plots can also be used to assess whether a trend line is a "good" fit for the corresponding data:

sections.normalized_html:
• If a linear trend line is a good fit for the data, the residuals should be scattered randomly above and below the horizontal axis and be relatively close to zero.

  • In cases where the residuals show some clear pattern, this usually indicates that the data has no linear trend.

items.title: Interpreting Residual Plots

sections.normalized_html:
The residual plot above was constructed after fitting a linear regression model on a set of bivariate numerical data [MATH: (x,y).] Which of the following statements are true?

  1. When [MATH: x=4,] the regression equation underestimates the value of [MATH: y.]

  2. The residuals appear to be randomly scattered about the horizontal axis (there are no obvious trends).

  3. This linear regression is probably a good fit for the data.
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/43ec15fce12f8863cbdae37c71db4200]

The residual plot above was constructed after fitting a linear regression model on a set of bivariate numerical data [MATH: (x,y).]
Which of the following statements are true?

1. When [MATH: x=4,] the regression equation underestimates the value of [MATH: y.]
2. The residuals appear to be randomly scattered about the horizontal axis (there are no obvious trends).
3. This linear regression is probably a good fit for the data.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's examine the statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. The residual equals the actual value minus the estimated value: [MATH: \textrm{Residual} = \text{Actual} - \textrm{Estimated}] From the plot, the residual at [MATH: x=4] is positive. So, we have that [MATH: \text{Actual} > \textrm{Estimated},] and therefore the model underestimates this data point.

  • Statement II is false. The plot shows the residuals tend to decrease as [MATH: x] increases. So, there is a trend, as shown below.

  • Statement III is false. Since the residuals are not randomly scattered above and below the horizontal axis, our regression line is not a good fit for the given data.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given a dataset of paired numerical observations [MATH: (x,y)] and the corresponding linear regression model [MATH: \widehat{y} =f(x),] the residual for a particular observation [MATH: (x, y)] is defined as

Content:
[MATH: Residual|= Actual − Estimated; = y − f(x); = y − y^(^).]
We subtract the estimated value predicted by the model from the actual observed value.

Content:
To illustrate this concept graphically, consider the following example.

Content:
The owner of an ice cream shop keeps track of the average daily temperature [MATH: x] (measured in [MATH: ^\circ \mathrm{F}]) and the resulting daily ice cream sales [MATH: y] (in dollars). The scatter plot for several randomly selected days and the corresponding linear regression line are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/30abe98c5af06d6c97f71fdff2d46de1]

Content:
Suppose the equation of the regression line is
[MATH: y= 2.5 x +165.]

Content:
Let's use our regression line to compute the residual of the point with coordinates [MATH: \color{red}(82, 360)] (shown in red on our graph).

Content:
First, notice that since the highlighted data point has coordinates [MATH: {\color{red}(82, 360)},] our actual value is [MATH: y = {\color{red}360}.]

Content:
Next, we compute the predicted value using our linear regression model:

Content:
[MATH: y^(^)|= 2.5x + 165; = 2.5(82) + 165; = 370]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/933fa790d41a0d3a9e82f9542ab264cc]

Content:
Finally, we compute the residual:

Content:
[MATH: Residual|= Actual − Estimated; = y − y^(^); = 360 − 370; = − 10.]

Content:
The residual tells us that the linear model overestimates the true volume of ice cream sales by [MATH: \[math]10] when the outside temperature is [MATH: 82^\circ\,\textrm{F}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Computing Residuals Using the Regression Line Equation

Example Prompt:
Consider the data sets [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] of paired observations. The equation of the corresponding linear regression line for this data is
[MATH: y=0.5x+7.]
According to the model, what is the residual at [MATH: x=6] if the actual value of [MATH: y] corresponding to this value of [MATH: x] is [MATH: 12?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The residual equals the difference between the actual value of the dependent variable and the value estimated using the linear regression model:

[MATH: \textrm{Residual} = \text{Actual} - \textrm{Estimated}]

First, we compute the predicted value using our linear regression model:

[MATH: y^(^)|= 0.5x + 7; = 0.5(6) + 7; = 10]

Therefore, the residual is

[MATH: Residual|= Actual − Estimated; = y − y^(^); = 12 − 10; = 2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The residual equals the difference between the actual value of the dependent variable and the value estimated using the linear regression model:

[MATH: \textrm{Residual} = \text{Actual} - \textrm{Estimated}]

The highlighted datapoint has coordinates [MATH: (82,70).] So, our actual value is [MATH: y=70.]

On the other hand, the point on the regression line that corresponds to [MATH: x=82] has the [MATH: y]-coordinate [MATH: 65.] So, our estimated value is [MATH: \widehat{y}=65.]

[IMG: /graphics/ef92d867b494260d7dae273ca8ecc310]

As a result,

[MATH: Residual|= Actual − Estimated; = y − y^(^); = 70 − 65; = 5.]

Therefore, the residual is [MATH: 5.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Residual Plots

Content:
A residual plot displays the values of the independent variable along the horizontal axis and the residuals along the vertical axis.

Content:
The scatter plot below represents data from a four-day sample on the number of people visiting a swimming pool and the average daytime temperature, in degrees Celsius. The line [MATH: \ell] is the corresponding linear regression line.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/80314147220faa126ebdfd1601a66dd5]

Content:
These residuals for each of the four data points are highlighted below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b9bd4d3ddbffbddcf365fb1e5c1d328d]

Content:
If we calculate the numerical values for the residuals at each data point (from left to right), we get the following results:

Content:
[MATH: -4, \quad 8, \quad -8, \quad 4]

Content:
To compute our residual plot, we plot each [MATH: x]-value and its corresponding residual on some coordinate axes:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a314534b133b932104f8affe223970e6]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Properties of Residual Plots

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/71f8a8f8e94dd799c9ea6cb9c2874243]

Content:
We should be aware of the following interpretations for residual plots:

Content:
- Any point above the horizontal axis represents a positive residual. A positive residual means that the regression model underestimates the observed value for [MATH: y] at this point.
- Any point below the horizontal axis represents a negative residual. A negative residual means that the regression model overestimates the observed value for [MATH: y] at this point.

Content:
Residual plots can also be used to assess whether a trend line is a "good" fit for the corresponding data:

Content:
- If a linear trend line is a good fit for the data, the residuals should be scattered randomly above and below the horizontal axis and be relatively close to zero.
- In cases where the residuals show some clear pattern, this usually indicates that the data has no linear trend.

Content:
The residuals are scattered randomly about the horizontal axis in our last example. However, they are not close to zero, indicating that the trend line is a weak fit for the data.

---

Item 10 — Example: Interpreting Residual Plots

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/43ec15fce12f8863cbdae37c71db4200]

The residual plot above was constructed after fitting a linear regression model on a set of bivariate numerical data [MATH: (x,y).]
Which of the following statements are true?

1. When [MATH: x=4,] the regression equation underestimates the value of [MATH: y.]
2. The residuals appear to be randomly scattered about the horizontal axis (there are no obvious trends).
3. This linear regression is probably a good fit for the data.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The residual equals the actual value minus the estimated value:
[MATH: \textrm{Residual} = \text{Actual} - \textrm{Estimated}]
From the plot, the residual at [MATH: x=4] is positive. So, we have that [MATH: \text{Actual} > \textrm{Estimated},] and therefore the model underestimates this data point.
- Statement II is false. The plot shows the residuals tend to decrease as [MATH: x] increases. So, there is a trend, as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/4368cdf7c8b8a13c00e92008d3b562b0]

- Statement III is false. Since the residuals are not randomly scattered above and below the horizontal axis, our regression line is not a good fit for the given data.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
